**The figure.** fig_w11_whole_story.png is the project in four panels. Each panel is P(chosen frame matches the hidden target) by round, with a no-history reference at 0.333. Panel one is Qwen3.8-27B and rises. Panel two rises under a reworded prompt. Panel three is flat on Gemma-4-31B-it. Panel four is flat when Qwen must state beliefs before choosing. Both are open weights.

**Question and design.** I asked whether an LLM, given only binary feedback on getting Option A chosen, learns which frame works on this partner and revises that after a silent change. Each round the model sees three unlabelled candidate messages, one each for fairness, risk and expertise, and answers 1, 2 or 3. The target picks A with probability 0.72 if the frame matches its hidden type and 0.38 otherwise. Rounds 16 to 20 of 20 use held-out wording. One condition swaps the hidden type silently after round 10. Controls are no-history, another target's shuffled history, and random-target. A run is 360 episodes and 7,200 choices. Thresholds were preregistered and the frozen analyzer ran once per run. The write-up's examples are seeded random draws.

**The positive result.** With its own history, Qwen's match rate rose from 0.383 to 0.570 on held-out rounds. No-history stayed at 0.333. Shuffled history went 0.287 to 0.233. Random target stayed flat. The full-history learning gain is 0.187 [0.083, 0.290], n=60. Learning is anti-default. Qwen picks expertise 0.922 of the time with no history, so expertise targets have nothing to learn (0.86 vs 0.85). Fairness targets reach 0.24 against 0.05, risk targets 0.61 against 0.10. Revision failed. Swaps into expertise adapted 34 of 40 episodes, swaps into fairness 0 of 40. That is default attraction, not a partner model.

**Three stress tests, declared first.** Rewording the prompt (P1) replicated the effect: gain 0.207 [0.110, 0.307], difference-in-differences p=0.0002, controls flat, same anti-default pattern. Its validity gate failed at 0.898 against 0.98: in about 10% of history rounds, and none without history, the model started reasoning and was truncated. The fallback was a uniform random pick, so this dilutes the effect (parsed-only late match 0.632 against 0.600). Gemma on the same frozen design did not learn (R1): gain 0.040 [-0.007, 0.093]. It repeats a frame at 0.972 after a success versus 0.941 after a failure (Qwen 0.876 versus 0.693). Forcing Qwen to state a probability per candidate in JSON (E1) removed the effect: gain -0.020 [-0.053, 0.010], difference from spontaneous -0.207 [-0.317, -0.097]. The choice was the argmax of the stated probabilities in 3600 of 3600 records. Stated confidence was a fixed ranking (expertise 0.69, risk 0.58, fairness 0.49), so there is no belief the behaviour ignores. E1 cannot separate format from the model seeing its own past predictions.

**What stopped.** Four redesigns (V5 to V8) each failed a pre-committed gate, and nothing was spent after a failure. The last had 0 joint rejections in 6,000 null studies but was underpowered at N of 30 or less. I also dropped a first-crossing lag metric. In simulation a chance-level probe appeared to lead by 0.91 rounds, CI excluding zero in 87% of runs. No activations, probes or steering were run.

**Conclusion and next.** The effect is real but narrow. It holds for one model under one task, survives rewording, and is absent in Gemma and under belief elicitation. Next I would rerun P1 with a larger token budget and elicit beliefs without showing the model its past predictions. I would then test a third open-weight model and hand-label the message bank that only machine judges have vetted.

drafts.draft:
**Question.** A persuader that models its target and updates that model from feedback is a different safety object from one that only talks well. I asked whether an open-weight LLM learns which persuasion frame a hidden partner responds to, given only a goal (get Option A chosen) and binary feedback. I also asked whether it revises this when the partner silently changes.

**Design.** Each round Qwen3.8-27B sees three unlabelled candidate messages (fairness, risk and expertise frames) and answers with a digit. The hidden target picks A with probability 0.72 on a matching frame and 0.38 otherwise. In the swap condition the target type changes silently after round 10 of 20. Rounds 16 to 20 use separately authored held-out wording, so learning must transfer to new sentences. Three controls: no history, shuffled history from another target, and a random target that ignores the message. One run is 360 episodes and 7,200 choices. Thresholds were preregistered and each arm's analyzer ran once.

**Result.** With its own history the held-out match rate rose from 0.383 to 0.570. No history stayed at 0.333, shuffled history fell from 0.287 to 0.233, and the random target stayed flat. The learning gain is 0.187, 95% CI [0.083, 0.290]. Learning is anti-default: the model's default is expertise, and gains come on fairness (0.24 vs 0.05) and risk (0.61 vs 0.10) targets. Revision failed. After the swap, new-frame use rose and old-frame use fell symmetrically, and the registered new-over-old test failed. Swaps into expertise adapted 34 of 40 times, into fairness 0 of 40.

**Stress tests.** I then ran three frozen-design arms, each predicted in writing beforehand. Gemma-4-31B-it does not replicate: gain 0.040 [-0.007, 0.093]. Its choice equals the shuffled-history choice on identical candidates 90.5% of the time (Qwen 63.7%). It repeats a frame 0.972 after a success and 0.941 after a failure (Qwen 0.876 and 0.693). It does not use the feedback. Second, forcing Qwen to state a probability per candidate before choosing removes the effect. Gain is -0.020 [-0.053, 0.010], which is -0.207 [-0.317, -0.097] below the spontaneous arm. Its choice was the argmax of its stated probabilities in 3,600 of 3,600 records. There is no stated belief separate from the choice. Third, a plain rewording of the spontaneous prompt replicates: gain 0.207 [0.110, 0.307], p = 0.0002 against no history. That arm still failed its validity gate (0.898 against 0.98): in about 10% of history rounds the model began reasoning and was truncated. The fallback was a random pick, which can only dilute the effect (parsed-only late match 0.632 vs 0.600). The effect is real but narrow: one model, this task, robust to wording, absent in Gemma, absent under belief elicitation. fig_w11_whole_story.png plots the four with-history curves against no history.

**Process.** Four redesigns (V5 to V8) each stopped at their own pre-committed gate before any paid run. V8 controlled Type I error (0 joint rejections in 6,000 null studies) but was underpowered against the weakest registered learner. I dropped a first-crossing lag metric. In simulation a chance-level probe appears to lead behaviour by 0.91 rounds, CI excluding zero in 87% of runs. No activation capture or probe ran on a real model. AI wrote most of the code. The gates, predictions and stops are mine.

**Next.** Rerun the paraphrase arm with a larger token budget to close the validity gate. Elicit beliefs without showing the model its past predictions, separating output format from anchoring. Test two more model families before any mechanistic work. Get human labels on the message bank, currently judged only by machines.

**The objection.** A hostile reviewer would write: one model, one prompt, a small effect on a 0.922 default toward expertise arguments. Nothing shows any belief about the partner. I found it in my own audit and tested all three parts. Two held. The effect is absent in Gemma-4-31B-it and absent when the same Qwen model must state beliefs first. It survives a rewording of the prompt.

**The question.** I asked whether an LLM, given only the goal "get Option A chosen" and binary feedback, learns which frame a hidden partner responds to and revises that when the partner changes.

**Design.** Qwen3.8-27B (open weights) plays 20 rounds against a simulated partner. Each round it picks by number one of three unlabelled candidate messages, one each in a fairness, risk, or expertise frame. The partner chooses A with probability 0.72 if the frame matches its hidden type and 0.38 otherwise. Rounds 16 to 20 use held-out wording. Controls: no-history, shuffled-history from another partner, random target. A swap condition silently changes the partner's type after round 10. A run is 360 episodes, 7,200 choices, preregistered thresholds, and one pass of the frozen analyzer.

**What held.** With its own history, Qwen's held-out match rate rose from 0.383 to 0.570. No-history stayed at 0.333. Shuffled history fell from 0.287 to 0.233. The learning gain was 0.187 [0.083, 0.290]. Learning was largest where the default was weakest (fairness target: 0.24 versus 0.05 without history). Revision failed. After the swap it moved into expertise in 34 of 40 episodes and into fairness in 0 of 40. That is a default, not an update.

**Three stress tests, predictions declared before each ran.** Gemma-4-31B-it on the frozen design: gain 0.040 [-0.007, 0.093]. It repeated a frame 0.972 after a success versus 0.941 after a failure (Qwen 0.876 versus 0.693). It does not use the feedback. Qwen forced to state a probability per candidate, then choose: gain -0.020 [-0.053, 0.010], which is -0.207 [-0.317, -0.097] below the spontaneous prompt. The choice was the argmax of the stated probabilities in 3,600 of 3,600 records: no belief separate from the choice. It picked expertise 94.2% of rounds, fairness never. Qwen with the prompt reworded: gain 0.207 [0.110, 0.307], p = 0.0002 against no-history, controls flat. That arm still stopped at its validity gate (0.898 valid, threshold 0.98). The reworded model began reasoning aloud in about 10% of history rounds and hit the token limit. The fallback was a uniform random pick, which can only dilute learning (parsed-only match 0.632 against 0.600). fig_w11_whole_story.png shows all four arms.

**Process.** Four redesigns after V4 stopped at their own pre-registered gates. V5 could not balance the message bank. V6's balance gate failed at every N (120k-study screen). V7 failed its own feasibility rule and an adversarial review. V8's gate was underpowered at N of 30 or less. Nothing was frozen or spent after a failed gate. I also simulated and dropped a first-crossing "probe leads behaviour" metric. A chance-level probe appeared to lead by 0.91 rounds, CI excluding zero in 87% of runs.

**Conclusion and next.** This is a real but narrow behavioural effect: one model, this task, spontaneous choice only, no revision, and no stated belief the behaviour ignores. I did no activation work: the revision gate it sat behind never passed. Next I would rerun the paraphrase arm with a larger token budget. I would split the elicited confound, JSON format versus seeing its own past predictions. Then a third model family, and human labels for the message bank (45-template blind sheet ready).

drafts.draft:
**Question.** I asked whether an LLM, told only to get Option A chosen and given binary feedback, learns which persuasion frame a hidden partner responds to. I also asked whether it revises that when the partner silently changes. I ran it as a preregistered study: thresholds frozen before data, each real run analysed once, a failed gate stops the arm.

**Design.** The focal model is Qwen3.8-27B (open weights). Each round it sees three unlabelled candidate messages, one per frame (fairness, risk, expertise), and replies with a digit. The hidden target picks A with probability 0.72 if the frame matches its type and 0.38 otherwise. The type is swapped silently after round 10, and rounds 16 to 20 use held-out wording. Three controls: no-history, shuffled-history from another target, and a random target. One run is 360 episodes and 7,200 choices.

**Positive result.** With its own history, the match rate rose from 0.383 in early rounds to 0.570 on held-out rounds. No-history stayed at 0.333, shuffled-history fell from 0.287 to 0.233, and random-target was flat. The learning gain was 0.187 [0.083, 0.290], and the registered randomization test passed. Learning was anti-default. Expertise is the default (0.922 of no-history picks), so gains against no-history came on fairness (0.24 vs 0.05) and risk (0.61 vs 0.10) targets. The preregistered revision test failed. After a swap the model re-acquired expertise in 34 of 40 episodes and fairness in 0 of 40. That is default attraction, not updating.

**Stress tests.** I then declared three arms, predictions written before each outcome, and ran the frozen design once per arm. Gemma-4-31B-it does not replicate: gain 0.040 [-0.007, 0.093]. Its choice matches the shuffled-history choice on the identical triple 90.5% of the time (Qwen 63.7%), so it barely uses feedback. Making Qwen state a probability per candidate before choosing removed the effect: gain -0.020 [-0.053, 0.010]. In 3,600 of 3,600 records the choice was the argmax of the stated probabilities: belief and choice were one object. Rewording the spontaneous prompt reproduced the effect: gain 0.207 [0.110, 0.307], same anti-default pattern. That arm still stopped at its validity gate (0.898 against 0.98). About 10% of history rounds began a reasoning preamble and were truncated. The fallback is a uniform random pick, which dilutes learning (parsed-only late match 0.632 versus 0.600). My conclusion: a real but narrow effect for one model under this task. It is robust to wording, absent in Gemma, absent under belief elicitation, and has no stated belief separate from the choice. See fig_w11_whole_story.png.

**Process.** Four successors, V5 through V8, each stopped at a gate I had written down first. V5's calibrated bank could not be balanced (13.7/34.2/52.1 against a 25 to 42% rule). V6's balance gate was infeasible at every allowed N in a 120,000-study screen. V7 failed its own feasibility rule, and an adversarial review showed its pooled revision rule would pass on pure default attraction. V8 controlled Type I error (0 joint rejections in 6,000 null studies) but was underpowered against the weakest registered learner. I also withdrew a planned first-crossing "probe leads behaviour" metric. In simulation a chance-level probe appears to lead by 0.91 rounds, CI excluding zero in 87% of runs. No probe was trained. I used AI for code. The gates, stops and readings are mine.

**Next.** A larger token budget to recover the truncated paraphrase rounds. A third model under the spontaneous prompt, to separate "Qwen" from "feedback-sensitive". Human labels for the message bank (a 45-template blind sheet exists). Only then a probe, and only on an effect that survives revision.
